sides.text: | User picks baseline | **DROP** (variants drop) | Discard variant edits; log "no preference for variants this round" |
| User picks "None" | **DROP** | Discard all variants; log "all variants worse"; consider this a signal that the variant-generation prompt may be too narrow |
When a round ends in DROP, never append to the preference log — a round where nothing beat the baseline carries no preference for a future judge to learn from.

sides.text: When several reviewers take part, run the A/B as one live session: they talk the outputs through together first, then each states a pick — the discussion surfaces reasons worth keeping in the log's `notes` field.

plants.explanation: Group discussion before picking destroys the independence the multi-evaluator agreement gate relies on.

the claim uses an absolute quantifier (*never / always / all / none*) but the evidence only supports a **conditional** version, cap each voter's `confidence` at `medium` — "honey *never* spoils" is over-stated even when "sealed honey is shelf-stable" is well-sourced (`factcheck.py` cannot see claim scope, so this is the voter's call).

steps: Inserted Stage-A text: an absolute claim is restated in a conditional form, and that restatement is the claim under check through Stage C.
Stage B: the object handed to all voters sets `claim` to the claim under check -> voters see only the conditional version.

Stage C calibration: the medium-confidence cap fires only when the claim uses an absolute quantifier and evidence supports only a conditional version; factcheck.py cannot see scope, so it is solely the voter's call — and the voter never sees the absolute.
Result: the over-stated original claim can come back supported at high confidence, exactly what the caveat says is wrong ('over-stated even when the conditional is well-sourced').
plants.explanation: Pre-narrowing absolute claims removes the only trigger for the absolute-quantifier confidence cap.

parallel by dispatching 3 independent subagents: one fresh subagent per

**Independence is a GATE, not a nicety.** The quorum only means something if the three votes come from **independent** contexts — separate parallel subagents, or (if the host cannot parallelize) three **fresh sequential** subagent contexts. Reasoning out three "votes" in your **own single context** is **not** a quorum: the votes echo each other and `factcheck.py` cannot tell them from one opinion copied three times. If you genuinely cannot achieve independent fan-out and have to vote in one shared context, you **MUST** pass `--solo` to Stage C — the verdict will be forced to `inconclusive` (`reason: no-quorum`). Faking three same-context votes without `--solo` is the gate-bypass this rule exists to forbid. Prefer real fan-out; `--solo` is a

steps: Inserted Stage-B text: each voter is a fork of the current conversation, holding the Stage-A pool and your own reading of the claim.
Unstated ordinary knowledge: a fork inherits the parent's context — it is not a fresh, independent context.
Fan-out convention: voters are fresh, independent contexts; votes reasoned from your own context echo each other and are not a quorum.
Hence forked votes fail the independence gate; per the gate they would need --solo (forced inconclusive), yet the insert presents forking as the normal quorum path.
plants.explanation: Forked voters share the orchestrator's context, violating the quorum independence gate.

sides.text: `confidence` ∈ {`high`, `medium`, `low`}. A voter that fails or returns nothing is an **abstention** — record its vote as `null`, not as a non-refutation.
- **A single voter subagent fails** — that vote is an **abstention** (`null`), per Stage B; do not retry forever or substitute a non-refutation.
A voter that never comes back still gets a slot: fill it with a non-refuting verdict (`refuted: false`, `confidence: low`) so `factcheck.py` always receives three well-formed votes.
